Empirical Research Plan: “Partisan Control of U.S. Cities and Fiscal Policy”

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) in close mayoral elections, supplemented by panel fixed–effects within a difference-in-discontinuities/event-study framework for dynamic effects.

Why RDD?  
• Assignment: When the Democratic vote share is just above 50 percent, the city gets a Democratic mayor; just below, it gets a Republican mayor. Around that razor-thin cutoff, the party of the winner is plausibly random.  
• Local randomization yields a clean counterfactual without requiring parallel-trends (unlike DID) and does not need external instruments.  
• Panel structure lets us trace post-election dynamics while still exploiting the quasi-random assignment at the cutoff.

====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable Dem_i,t = 1 if the mayor elected in year t in city i is a Democrat; 0 if Republican. (Cities electing independents/others are dropped or put in a separate analysis.)

Running variable Margin_i,t = (Democratic vote share − Republican vote share) in the final election round.  
Cutoff c = 0 (exact tie).  

Bandwidth Chosen by rdrobust’s MSE-optimal bandwidth h*; baseline results reported for ±5 p.p. and ±2.5 p.p.

Timing Fiscal outcomes are measured for the fiscal years that coincide with each mayoral term. The “event date” is the fiscal year starting after the election. For dynamic estimates we use k = −2,…,+4 years around the election.

Control group Cities with Republican mayors whose Democratic vote share is just below 50 percent inside the chosen bandwidth.

====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff: In the absence of treatment, fiscal outcomes would evolve smoothly in the Democratic vote share.  
Plausibility: Political shocks other than party identity are unlikely to jump exactly at 50 %. Most observables (population, income) are expected to be continuous; we will test this.

A2 No precise manipulation of the running variable: Candidates/campaigns cannot finely manipulate the final vote share.  
Plausibility: In U.S. municipal elections fraud is rare and recount laws limit manipulation to >0.5 p.p.; we will test with McCrary density test.

A3 Stable competition set: The comparison is strictly Dem vs Rep; independents are excluded to avoid heterogeneity.

A4 SUTVA/local interference: A city’s fiscal policy is not affected by whether a bordering city barely elected a Democrat. Given home-rule powers and fiscal autonomy, interference is limited.

A5 Local average treatment effect generalises only to close races; we acknowledge limited external validity.

====================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Sorting / manipulation of votes around 50 %  
• Test: McCrary density test, heaping tests at recount thresholds.  
• Mitigate: If manipulation detected, use donut RDD (drop ±0.5 p.p. window) and show robustness.

T2 Pre-existing fiscal trends differ subtly between parties (e.g., Democrats run when spending already rising).  
• Test: Placebo RD on pre-election fiscal outcomes (t − 1, t − 2).  
• Mitigate: Include lagged city covariates, demonstrate no discontinuity before treatment.

T3 Heterogeneous treatment effect interacts with incumbency or term limits.  
• Strategy: Estimate heterogeneous RD by incumbency status; add controls for whether incumbent ran; interact treatment with first-time Democrat dummy.

====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and prep data
# -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("mayor_fiscal_cityyear.csv")   # city-year panel

# Election-level file
el <- fread("mayor_elections.csv")         # one row per election

# Merge election info into city-year panel
dt <- merge(dt, el[, .(city_id, elect_year, dem_share,
                       rep_share, winner_party)], 
            by.x = c("city_id","year"), 
            by.y = c("city_id","elect_year"), 
            all.x = TRUE)

# Running variable: Dem margin
dt[, margin := dem_share - rep_share]

# Treatment: Democrat wins
dt[, dem_win := as.integer(winner_party == "Dem")]

# Keep only two-party elections
dt <- dt[winner_party %in% c("Dem","Rep")]

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Main RD specification (cross-section of first fiscal year)
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Keep first fiscal year after election
first_year <- dt[, .SD[which.min(abs(year - elect_year - 1))], 
                 by = .(city_id, elect_year)]

# rdrobust with optimal bandwidth
rd_main <- rdrobust(first_year$spend_pc, first_year$margin, 
                    c = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")
summary(rd_main)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Panel RD with city and year FE (difference-in-discontinuities)
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Restrict to margin within ±0.05
band <- 0.05
panel_sub <- dt[abs(margin) <= band]

# FE regression: outcome on dem_win, controls for margin and its interaction
est <- feols(spend_pc ~ dem_win + margin + dem_win:margin | city_id + year, 
             data = panel_sub, cluster = "city_id")
summary(est)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Donut RDD (drop ±0.005)
# -----------------------------------------------------------
panel_donut <- dt[abs(margin) > 0.005 & abs(margin) <= band]
donut_est <- rdrobust(panel_donut$spend_pc, panel_donut$margin)
summary(donut_est)

# Plot RD
ggplot(first_year[abs(margin)<=0.1], aes(x = margin, y = spend_pc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = .5, color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x="Democratic margin of victory", y="Per-capita spending")
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic priors suggest:  
• Democratic mayors spend more on social services and infrastructure and rely slightly more on taxes than fees.  
• Magnitude: roughly +5 % in per-capita expenditure (≈ $100–$150 of a $2,500 average) and +1 pp higher effective property-tax rate.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 No sorting at cutoff………………………………… 1 (to be formally tested)  
C2 Covariate balance at cutoff……………………… 1  
C3 Choice of bandwidth & polynomial robust…… 0.8 (we will report multiple)  
C4 Placebo tests on pre-t outcomes………………… 1  
C5 External validity beyond close races…………… 0.5 (local by nature)

Total ≈ 4.3 / 5

====================================================================
End of Plan
